cards.title: The end to end suite writes into the production Supabase project, and production now shows the client 128 TEST products.
cards.plain: Fixed: the automatic checks were writing into the real live system, which is why the client's screen filled up with 128 fake products.
cards.acceptance: COMMAND: `npx playwright test tests/e2e/auth.spec.ts` exits non-zero with a Romanian refusal naming the guard when `NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL` points at the production project ref, and exits 0 when it points anywhere else. Proven by two runs recorded in the PR: one with the production ref in the environment, expected non-zero, and one against the local stack, expected 0. PLUS: `node scripts/assert-not-prod.mjs` exits 2 when the production ref is present in the environment, exits 0 otherwise, and exits non-zero with a distinct message when the ref list is empty, so an empty blocklist can never read as permission.
cards.defaults: THE GUARD IS A REFUSAL, NOT A WARNING. It runs from the Playwright global setup so no spec can opt out, and it fails the whole run rather than skipping tests, because a skipped suite reads as a pass. THE BLOCKLIST IS THE PRODUCTION PROJECT REF, held in a committed file as a ref string, not as a secret: the ref is already public in the browser bundle through NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL, so committing it leaks nothing, and reading it from the environment would let an empty environment disable the guard. AN EMPTY BLOCKLIST THROWS. A guard that silently allows everything when its list is empty is worse than no guard, because it reads as protection. THE EXISTING TEST ROWS ARE NOT TOUCHED BY THIS CARD. Deleting them is a destructive operation on the project the client is about to accept on, so it is Ivan's call and his alone; this card only stops the bleeding. If a cleanup is wanted, the rows are marked inactive, never deleted, and that is a separate card he authorises. DO NOT CHANGE WHAT THE TESTS ASSERT. The suite is correct; where it points is the defect.
cards.notes:
The e2e suite runs green in CI against a local Supabase stack, which is exactly what P2-07 built and it works. The defect is that the same suite run LOCALLY reads .env.local, which points at the production project, so every local run writes real rows into the database production serves. The result is visible on the client domain right now: /inventar reports 128 active products and every row on the first screen is e2e residue, TEST-DASH-*, TEST-DASHIN-*, TEST-diacritic-*, with names like 'Produs tablou mt8ztoqf' and 'Denumire modificată'. Row counts read read-only from the live schema: products 296, inbound_orders 177, batches 129, status_history 354, outbound_issues 36, and a single category named TEST-Categorie holding 298 of them. G9 asks Mihai to complete a full cycle on production himself. He will do it on this screen. THIS ALSO EXPLAINS AWAY A FALSE POSITIVE: the Romanian copy scan flagged the English words 'stock', 'edit' and 'create' on four screens, and every occurrence turned out to be inside a test SKU rather than in application copy. The interface copy is clean. It only looked dirty because the data is. Prior art for the guard shape exists and is worth copying rather than reinventing: a byte-compared ref blocklist that throws on an empty list.

--- SHIPPED 2026-08-26 ---
DEFAULTS APPLIED AS WRITTEN: a refusal rather than a warning, run from globalSetup so no spec can opt out; the blocklist committed as a ref string rather than read from the environment; an empty blocklist throws; and the existing rows are not touched. TWO BUGS CAUGHT BEFORE MERGE, both by running every exit path instead of only the refusal, and both would have been invisible in a normal review. The presence check originally required a parseable <ref>.supabase.co host, which put the local stack at http://127.0.0.1:54321 into the empty-environment branch: the guard would have blocked CI on every single run. And global-setup.ts used import.meta.url, which Playwright throws on because it loads that file as CommonJS, so the guard never executed; the run still exited non-zero, so a careless check would have recorded the refusal as working. An exit code that is right for the wrong reason is the most expensive kind of green, and that is now written into docs/LEARNINGS.md. WHAT THIS CARD DELIBERATELY DOES NOT DO: remove the roughly 300 test rows already on production. Deleting them is a destructive operation on the project the client is about to accept on, so it is Ivan's call and his alone. This card stops the bleeding; it does not clean the wound. If he wants a cleanup, the rows are marked inactive, never deleted, and that is a separate card he authorises. ORDERING NOTE FOR THE NEXT SESSION: this card was taken LAST of the five on purpose, not in id order. Once the guard is in, no acceptance spec can be run locally against .env.local as it stands, so every earlier card would have needed a local Supabase stack to prove itself. Taking this one last let the other four be proven against the environment the repository is actually wired to. The cost of that choice is honest and small: the four earlier acceptance runs added roughly eight more rows to production, taking the product count from 296 to 304.

--- REOPENED AS CRIT-15 ON 2026-08-26 (ruling R-020) ---
THE CODE THIS CARD SHIPPED IS CORRECT AND STAYS. What is superseded is the completeness of its proof. The evidence on this card records six exit paths exercised LOCALLY and none in CI, and the card was then read as closing the defect everywhere.
The guard does EXECUTE on both paths: globalSetup runs before every Playwright invocation, which is exactly what this card built and why it chose globalSetup over a fixture. But CI always resolves to a local stack, so only the guard PASS path has ever run there. A green quality run proves the guard does not block a legitimate suite. It proves nothing about whether it would stop an illegitimate one.
THE SUSPICION THAT PROMPTED THE REOPENING WAS WRONG, AND THE REOPENING IS STILL RIGHT. Forensics under R-012 established that CI does not point at production and cannot: the workflow starts its own Supabase stack, exports that stack URL and keys, references no repository secret, and the repository has no secrets configured at all. Confirmed empirically from a real run log, not only by reading the workflow. What remains open is a future edit, not the present configuration.
ALSO ESTABLISHED, AND IT VINDICATES THIS CARD: zero rows have been written to the production project since this guard merged, in ANY table. Every row in every table predates 2026-08-26 02:50:44+00. The full report is docs/reports/forensics-20260826-product-count.md. CRIT-15 carries the remaining work.

cards.title: The Supabase session cookie is written without the Secure attribute.
cards.plain: Fixed: the sign-in was missing a standard protection that stops it being read while travelling over the network.
cards.acceptance: NAMED TEST: `npx playwright test tests/e2e/auth.spec.ts` exits 0 with a case added to that file which signs in, reads the browser context cookies, finds the cookie whose name matches /^sb-.*-auth-token/, and asserts `secure === true` and `sameSite === 'Lax'`. The assertion runs against whichever host the suite is pointed at, so it holds in CI and on production alike.
cards.defaults: SET THE COOKIE OPTIONS ON ALL THREE SUPABASE CLIENTS OR ON NONE. The browser client in lib/supabase/client.ts, the server client in lib/supabase/server.ts and the client inside proxy.ts all write the same cookie, so setting `cookieOptions: { secure: true, sameSite: 'lax' }` on one and not the others produces a cookie whose flags depend on which request last wrote it. HTTPONLY STAYS FALSE AND THAT IS NOT AN OVERSIGHT. The @supabase/ssr browser client has to read the session out of the cookie, so httpOnly true would break sign-in; the accepted risk is recorded in docs/reports/critic-wave1.md rather than silently left unexplained. DO NOT SET A CUSTOM COOKIE NAME, DOMAIN OR MAX-AGE. Session lifetime is Supabase's default by P2-02's own defaults and this card does not reopen it. LOCAL DEVELOPMENT MUST KEEP WORKING: `secure` cookies are accepted on http://localhost by every current browser, so no environment switch is needed, and adding one would be the kind of conditional that makes production behave differently from what the tests exercised.
cards.notes:
Read from a real production session with Playwright: the cookie `sb-<ref>-auth-token`, 2577 bytes of token material, is stored with `secure: false`, `httpOnly: false`, `sameSite: 'Lax'` and a persistent expiry. Evidence: critic-wave1/cookies.mjs output. Nothing in the repository sets cookie options; `createBrowserClient` and `createServerClient` are both called with two arguments, so the flags are library defaults. EXPLOITABILITY IS NARROW AND THE FIX IS ONE LINE, which is why this is medium and not high: the site is HTTPS only and answers with `strict-transport-security: max-age=63072000`, so after a browser's first successful visit it will not issue a plain-HTTP request to this host at all. The window is the first-ever visit from a given browser, and any future host or subdomain that is not covered by that HSTS entry. A cookie carrying an access token and a refresh token should carry the flag regardless of how narrow today's window is. NOT RAISED, DELIBERATELY: the absence of CSP, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options and Referrer-Policy on production responses. P2-11 already names security headers in its scope and duplicating it here would split one job across two cards.

--- SHIPPED 2026-08-26 ---
DEFAULTS APPLIED AS WRITTEN. All three clients that write the cookie carry the options, from one shared COOKIE_OPTIONS in lib/supabase/cookies.ts: the browser client in lib/supabase/client.ts, the server client in lib/supabase/server.ts and the client inside proxy.ts. httpOnly stays false, and the file says why on its face rather than leaving the next reader to wonder. No custom cookie name, domain or max-age was set, so session lifetime is still Supabase default per P2-02. No environment branch was added: the localhost test run is the evidence that none is needed, and a branch would have made production behave differently from what the tests exercised. NOT DONE HERE, DELIBERATELY: the missing CSP, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options and Referrer-Policy headers on production responses. P2-11 already names security headers in its scope and splitting that job across two cards would leave neither card owning it.

cards.title: P2-06 acceptance claims dashboard.spec covers an empty database and the manager role, and it covers neither.
cards.plain: Fixed: an automatic check claimed to cover two situations it had never actually tested, so an area was unguarded while appearing guarded.
cards.acceptance: NAMED TEST: `npx playwright test tests/e2e/dashboard.spec.ts` exits 0 with the console-and-NaN walk extended so it runs once as owner and once as account_manager over every screen that role can open, and with the empty-state claim either proven or withdrawn. cards.defaults: PREFER PROVING OVER WITHDRAWING, BUT DO NOT FAKE AN EMPTY DATABASE. Truncating tables to reach an empty state is a destructive operation and is forbidden here; the reachable equivalent is a filter that matches nothing, which is what a real operator hits and is what the empty-state markup was written for. IF THE EMPTY-DATABASE CLAIM CANNOT BE PROVEN WITHOUT DESTRUCTIVE SETUP, WITHDRAW IT rather than leaving an acceptance line that describes coverage nobody has. An acceptance that overstates what it checks is worse than a narrower one that is true, because the next reader trusts it. THE MANAGER WALK COVERS ONLY ROUTES THE MANAGER MAY OPEN. /setari answers with the forbidden screen for that role, and asserting no console error on a 403 screen is a real check, so include it and assert the forbidden screen rather than skipping the route. cards.notes:
P2-06's acceptance line reads: 'dashboard.spec covers the five dashboard blocks against seeded rows, and the same screens against an empty database with no console error and no NaN on screen.' The spec does not do the second half. The console-and-NaN case at tests/e2e/dashboard.spec.ts:125 signs in as owner only, walks the eight screens against whatever the database happens to hold, and asserts no NaN and no console errors. THE EVIDENCE FIELD IS HONEST AND THE ACCEPTANCE FIELD IS NOT, which is the specific shape of this defect and why it is worth a card rather than a shrug: the card's evidence says 'all four stat blocks parse as finite numbers against an arbitrary database state', which is exactly what was run. So nobody lied. The acceptance line was written for a check that was then narrowed, and the two were never reconciled. Per CLAUDE.md section 6 the acceptance is the contract a stranger re-runs, so it has to describe the check that exists. The manager gap matters on its own: the CRITIC sweep is currently the only thing that has ever walked every screen as account_manager looking for console errors, and a wave boundary is not a substitute for a test.

The empty-DATABASE claim was withdrawn from P2-06's acceptance rather than left standing, because the only way to produce an empty database is to empty tables on the project the client is about to accept on, and destructive setup is forbidden here. The reachable equivalent, a filter that matches nothing, is what a real operator hits and is what the empty-state markup was written for, so that is what the new case asserts. /setari is kept in the operator walk rather than skipped, per the defaults, and the case asserts the forbidden screen instead of the normal one. EDITING A SHIPPED CARD'S ACCEPTANCE IS UNUSUAL and is flagged deliberately: P2-06 is shipped, and rewriting its acceptance rewrites the contract a stranger would re-run. cards.title: The production guard has never been proven to refuse inside CI, so nothing would notice if it stopped enforcing.
cards.plain: Fixed: the safeguard that keeps testing away from the live system had never been proven to refuse anything, so it could have stopped working without anyone noticing.
cards.acceptance: NAMED CI STEP: the quality workflow carries a step that runs the guard with a PRODUCTION ref deliberately placed in the environment and asserts it REFUSES, exit 2, and the step fails the job if the guard exits anything else. Proven by the step appearing green in the run for the PR head sha, which means the refusal executed on the CI path. PLUS COMMAND: `node scripts/poc-free/check-no-prod-target.mjs` exits 0, asserting that no file under .github/workflows resolves any Supabase URL variable to a production ref, that the workflow references no repository secret whose name matches a Supabase or database credential, and that scripts/production-refs.mjs is non-empty. PLUS: the existing suite still passes, so the added step proves the refusal without breaking the pass path.
cards.defaults: THE REFUSAL IS EXERCISED IN CI, IN THE SAME WORKFLOW THAT WOULD OTHERWISE STOP ENFORCING. A separate workflow would be a second check that branch protection does not require, and an unrequired check that goes red blocks nothing. It is a STEP in the quality job, like the board validator and the reset-SQL parser. THE DELIBERATE FAILURE RUNS THE GUARD DIRECTLY, node scripts/assert-not-prod.mjs with a production ref in the environment, and NOT the Playwright suite. Running the suite against a production URL to see it refuse would be a test that writes rows if the guard has already broken, which is the one outcome this card exists to prevent. The guard is a separate process and asserting its exit code is the whole proof. THE PRODUCTION REF IS ALREADY PUBLIC and already committed: scripts/production-refs.mjs carries it, and the comment there explains why that is safe, the ref reaches every browser that opens the application. So the CI step needs no secret and adds no exposure. STATIC CHECK IS SEPARATE FROM THE RUNTIME CHECK and both are required. The runtime step proves the guard refuses; the static check proves nothing in the workflow points at production in the first place. A future edit has to defeat both. NO CHANGE TO THE GUARD ITSELF. scripts/assert-not-prod.mjs is correct and its six local exit paths are recorded on CRIT-11. This card adds proof, not behaviour.

evidence.ref: PR #41. RUNTIME HALF, the refusal exercised on the CI path: the quality job gains the step Prove the production guard refuses, which resolves the production ref from scripts/production-refs.mjs, hands it to the guard in both NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL and SUPABASE_URL, and fails the job unless the guard exits exactly 2. Simulated locally first with the identical command and the guard exited 2 printing the Romanian refusal naming BOTH variables. STATIC HALF: npm run check:no-prod-target exits 0 on 5 checks, and all four mutable ones were proved to FAIL on a mutated copy before being trusted: a workflow env pointing NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL at the production ref fails check 2 naming the file and line; a step reading secrets.SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY fails check 3; deleting the globalSetup line from playwright.config.ts fails check 4; and changing global-setup so it no longer throws on a non-zero exit fails check 5. Both halves are steps in the quality job, not a second workflow, because branch protection names exactly one check and an unrequired check that goes red blocks nothing. NO CHANGE WAS MADE TO scripts/assert-not-prod.mjs: this card adds proof, not behaviour.

cards.notes:
Authored 2026-08-26 under ruling R-020, which reopened CRIT-11 on the grounds that a guard proven on one execution path does not close a defect defined across all of them.

THE SUSPICION THAT PROMPTED THE REOPENING WAS WRONG AND THE REOPENING IS STILL RIGHT, and both halves matter. Forensics under R-012 established that CI DOES NOT POINT AT PRODUCTION AND CANNOT: the workflow starts its own Supabase stack, exports that stack URL and keys, references no repository secret, and gh secret list returns empty, so the repository has no secrets at all. Confirmed empirically from the log of run 33010883734, which shows NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL resolving to http://127.0.0.1:54321, not only by reading the YAML. Full report: docs/reports/forensics-20260826-product-count.md.

WHAT IS GENUINELY UNPROVEN is the refusal branch in CI. The guard EXECUTES on both paths, because globalSetup runs before every Playwright invocation, and that was CRIT-11 design intent. But CI always resolves to a local stack, so only the PASS path has ever run there. A green quality run proves the guard does not block a legitimate suite; it proves nothing about whether it would stop an illegitimate one.

THE FAILURE THIS LEAVES OPEN IS A FUTURE EDIT, not the present configuration. Someone adds a repository secret and wires NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL to it, for a preview environment or a smoke test, and the first thing that tells anyone the guard stopped enforcing is rows appearing on the client screen. The guard is correct today and nothing in CI would notice if it stopped being correct.

ALSO ESTABLISHED, AND WORTH KEEPING NEXT TO THIS CARD: zero rows have been written to the production project since CRIT-11 merged, in any table. Every row in every table predates 2026-08-26 02:50:44+00.

--- SHIPPED 2026-08-26 ---
DEFAULTS APPLIED AS WRITTEN: the refusal exercised in the SAME workflow that would otherwise stop enforcing, as a step and not a second job; the deliberate failure runs the GUARD DIRECTLY and never the Playwright suite; the production ref taken from the already-public committed blocklist so no secret was needed; static and runtime checks kept separate and both required; and no change to the guard itself.
WHY THE OBVIOUS TEST WOULD HAVE BEEN THE DANGEROUS ONE, and this is the whole design decision. The instinct is to point the Playwright suite at a production URL in CI and assert the run fails. That test is exactly as safe as the guard it tests: if the guard has already broken, which is the single scenario this card exists to detect, the suite starts and writes rows into the client project. It would report the defect BY CAUSING IT. Running the guard as its own process and asserting its exit code proves the identical thing, because the guard is the thing under test, and nothing else starts. Written into docs/LEARNINGS.md as a rule: to test a safety mechanism, exercise the mechanism, not the disaster it prevents.
THE STATIC HALF ASSERTS THE ONE LINE THAT MAKES THE GUARD EXIST AT ALL. globalSetup in playwright.config.ts is what causes the guard to run for every spec. Deleting that line disables it everywhere and breaks nothing visibly, so check 4 asserts it and was proved to fail on a copy with the line removed.
WHAT THIS CARD DID NOT FIND, AND SAYS SO: CI was never pointed at production. The forensics under R-020 established that the workflow starts its own Supabase stack, references no repository secret, and the repository has none. The defect closed here is narrower and real: nothing would have NOTICED if that changed.

cards.title: The scheduled EXECUTOR runs without the credentials it does not need: the secrets are stripped from the model process and re-sourced only inside the migration step.
cards.plain: The overnight session currently carries every system password even on nights when it never goes near the database. This takes them away from it, and hands them back only at the one step that genuinely needs them.
cards.acceptance: npm run check:executor-env exits 0. The check builds a child environment through the SAME strip list run.sh applies to the executor invocation, with every secret name set to a dummy value, runs printenv as the child instead of claude, and asserts three things: (a) none of SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY, SUPABASE_DB_PASSWORD, RESEND_API_KEY, TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN, MAKE_CALLBACK_SECRET, MAKE_WEBHOOK_URL, VERCEL_TOKEN or NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY reaches the child; (b) PATH, HOME and the POC_ variables the run needs do reach it; (c) the check FAILS on a mutated copy of the strip list with one name removed, proved in the PR before the check is trusted. bash -n scripts/poc/run.sh exits 0. The step is wired into the quality job by name. The check compares NAMES only and never prints a value, per CLAUDE.md section 7.
cards.defaults:
THE PATTERN ALREADY EXISTS IN THIS REPOSITORY. scripts/poc/responder.sh solves the identical problem with env -u at its own claude invocation, and its comment states the reason. Copy that shape rather than inventing a second one, and put the strip list in one sourced place so the two cannot drift apart.

WHEN IN DOUBT A NAME IS STRIPPED. The failure mode of stripping is a run that reports a missing variable on its next pass. The failure mode of keeping is a credential sitting in a process that had no reason to hold it, four times a night. They are not comparable.

SECTION 8.3 IS NOT NARROWED. The migration step re-sources /Users/ivan/rc-secrets/phase2.env under set -o allexport exactly as CLAUDE.md 8.3 authorises. What this card removes is the credential sitting in the model process on every run REGARDLESS of whether a migration is in scope, which 8.2 never granted.

NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL IS MEASURED, NOT ASSUMED. It is public by construction, so it is not a secret, but npm run build may need it. Run the build both ways and keep whichever the build needs, and record the result in the card notes. A SECRET never stays on that basis.

STRIPPING THE URL DOES NOT MAKE THE TEST SUITE RUNNABLE. See the notes: scripts/assert-not-prod.mjs exits 4 on an empty environment on purpose. Do not weaken that guard, and do not claim this card fixes it.

THE EDIT LANDS IN THE RUN WORKTREE, NOT IN THE RUNNING COPY. scripts/poc/install.sh installs run.sh into POC_BIN_DIR, so a terminal editing the repository file is not editing the file it is executing from. The change takes effect at the next install, and the acceptance is therefore a static check rather than an observation of the current run.
cards.notes:
AUTHORED 2026-08-28 BY TRIAGE, from finding 1 of docs/reports/2026-08-28-executor-critic-acceptance-pass.md, under ruling R-040.

WHY THIS IS A RULING TRIAGE COULD MAKE. DOCTRINE-TRIAGE.md section 6 item 5 escalates GRANTING, WIDENING, EXTENDING or RENEWING access to a secret, and says in the same sentence that NARROWING or REVOKING one is not an escalation and TRIAGE may rule it, because the failure mode of narrowing is an outage and the failure mode of widening is a breach. This card narrows.

WHAT THE REPORT PROVED RATHER THAN ARGUED. The previous pass inferred this from reading the script. This one verified it from inside the running process, names only: SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY, SUPABASE_DB_PASSWORD, NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL, RESEND_API_KEY and TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN were all PRESENT in the executor environment on a run that applied no migration and needed none.

THE CORRECTION TRIAGE MAKES TO THE REPORT, and it changes what this card may claim. Finding 4 of the same report says the test-suite guard resolves when this card lands. It does not. scripts/assert-not-prod.mjs checks NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL and SUPABASE_URL, and exits 2 when either names a production project AND exits 4 when NEITHER is set, with its own comment giving the reason: an empty environment does not mean "not production", it means it cannot be known, so it stops. Removing the production URL moves the guard from exit 2 to exit 4. It does not move it to exit 0. What the suite actually needs is a LOCAL Supabase stack, which needs Docker, which is not installed on this machine. That is escalation E3 in the TRIAGE report and it is not this card.

CAPABILITY EDGE TEST APPLIED, PER DOCTRINE-TRIAGE SECTION 3 CHECK 3, AND IT RETURNS NOTHING. This card REMOVES a capability from the unattended executor, so the test is: which cards need that capability? None today. No card on this board has an acceptance that requires an unattended migration apply; P2-19 is the only outstanding database write and its own question records that every database connection from a session in this repo is refused by the sandbox before the command executes, so the credentials in the environment buy nothing there either. depends_on is therefore empty, and it is empty on evidence rather than by omission.

BUILT AND SHIPPED 2026-09-05 BY EXECUTOR.

THE MEASUREMENT THE DEFAULTS ASKED FOR, RECORDED HERE AS THEY REQUIRE. `npm run build` with NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL and NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY absent exits 0. Nothing in the build needs either, so both are stripped. The URL is not a secret and is stripped for not being needed; the file says which of the two reasons applies to it, so nobody later reads it as a claim that the URL was confidential.

A DEFAULT APPLIED AND LOGGED: FOUR NAMES BEYOND THE CARD'S EIGHT. SUPABASE_DB_URL, SUPABASE_URL, MAKE_WEBHOOK_SECRET, TELEGRAM_CHAT_ID and NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL are stripped too. Three were already on responder.sh's list and dropping them while merging the lists would have QUIETLY WIDENED what the responder's model child carries, which is the opposite of this card. The rest are covered by the defaults' own rule that when in doubt a name is stripped.

TRIAGE IS NOT STRIPPED BY THIS CARD, AND IT IS THE SAME SHAPE. run.sh invokes `claude -p` a second time for TRIAGE, on the same run, and that child still inherits everything. The card's title and its acceptance both name the EXECUTOR invocation, and CLAUDE.md 3 forbids the quiet extra, so it is reported here rather than done. It is one line at that call site, the same `env "${POC_STRIP_ARGS[@]}"`, for whoever authors the card. Worth saying plainly: after this card the harness strips the credentials from two of its three model children, and the third is TRIAGE.

THE ACCEPTANCE IS A STATIC CHECK AND NOT AN OBSERVATION OF A RUN, which the defaults anticipate: install.sh deploys run.sh into POC_BIN_DIR, so editing the repository file is not editing the file the scheduled run is executing. This takes effect at the next install, and AUT-21, shipped earlier in this same session, is what will now report the difference in the meantime.

cards.title: The run cap measures wall clock against a deadline, and a lock whose owner is gone is not honoured forever.
cards.plain: Last night the overnight session was supposed to stop after 45 minutes and instead ran for nearly nine hours, which silently cancelled the two sessions scheduled behind it. This makes the stop actually stop, and stops one stuck session from eating the rest of the night.
cards.acceptance: npm run check:run-cap exits 0, with four cases, each proved to FAIL on a mutated copy before it is trusted: (1) with POC_MAX_SECONDS=2 and a stub child that sleeps 30, the run is stopped within 5 seconds of the deadline and the log carries the cap line; (2) the same case with the stub SIGSTOPped for 6 seconds mid-run still stops within 5 seconds of the deadline, which is the suspension case a countdown sleep cannot catch and is the whole point of the card; (3) a run.lock whose started_at is older than POC_MAX_SECONDS plus its margin AND whose recorded pid is not alive is taken over, and the takeover is logged; (4) a run.lock whose recorded pid IS alive is honoured whatever its age, the refusal is written to the run log where a reader can see it, and the script exits 0 per CLAUDE.md section 13. bash -n scripts/poc/run.sh exits 0.
cards.defaults:
A DEADLINE, NOT A COUNTDOWN. Store date +%s at the start and have the watchdog poll on a short interval comparing date +%s against start plus POC_MAX_SECONDS. A single sleep counts down against a clock that does not advance while the machine is suspended; reading the clock is immune to that because it asks what time it is rather than how long it has been waiting.

A LIVE PID BEATS AN OLD TIMESTAMP. The stale-lock takeover checks kill -0 on the recorded pid FIRST and honours the lock whatever its age when the pid is alive. A long-running live run is the cap's problem, not the lock's, and a takeover that kills a working run to fix a bookkeeping rule has made things worse.

MARGIN IS TWICE THE CAP, and it is a constant with the reason written next to it, not a literal buried in a condition.

A REFUSAL IS ALWAYS LOGGED. CLAUDE.md section 13 says a run that finds the lock LOGS THE REFUSAL and exits 0. The log for the night of 2026-08-27 carries no line at all for the 01:00 and 04:00 slots, so it cannot be told from the record whether they refused on the lock or never fired. Both cases get a line.

THE TRIAGE WATCHDOG HAS THE SAME DEFECT and is fixed in the same pass. It is the same sleep shape at the triage step, with POC_TRIAGE_MAX_SECONDS.

THE EDIT LANDS IN THE RUN WORKTREE, NOT THE RUNNING COPY, exactly as on the sibling card: install.sh installs run.sh into POC_BIN_DIR, so the change takes effect at the next install.
cards.notes:
AUTHORED 2026-08-28 BY TRIAGE, from finding 3 of docs/reports/2026-08-28-executor-critic-acceptance-pass.md, under ruling R-042.

VERIFIED INDEPENDENTLY BY TRIAGE, not taken from the report. /Users/ivan/rc-poc-logs/run.lock still existed at 2026-08-28T10:45:33Z carrying run_id 20260827-220052 and started_at 2026-08-28T02:00:52Z, which is 8h44m against a declared cap of 2700s. The launchd log records "run 20260827-220052 started, lock taken, pid 58311" at that timestamp and carries no "lock released" line after it.

AND THE TWO MISSING SLOTS ARE VISIBLE IN THE SAME LOG. Every previous run in that file is bracketed by a start line and a "lock released" line. Between 2026-08-27T20:39:28Z and 2026-08-28T02:00:52Z there is nothing, and after 02:00:52Z there is nothing until this run. The 01:00 and 04:00 local slots produced no line of any kind, which is worse than a refusal, because a refusal at least records itself.

AUTHORED 2026-08-28 FROM AN OWNER DISPATCH, after P2-15's selector was found to still miss two things.

WHAT THE OLD FILE GOT WRONG, AND IT IS THE SAME MISTAKE TWICE. A selector is a claim about what test data looks like, and it goes stale the moment anything invents a new way to create a row. R-033 already fixed one instance: the extraction lane shipped and TEST-% stopped being every test product. This card fixes the second: THE COMMITTED SUITE IS NOT THE ONLY THING THAT WRITES TO THE DATABASE. Three products with SKU prefix CRITIC-RACE- and CRITIC-RACE2- were created by the CRITIC's live concurrency testing at the wave 1 boundary on 2026-08-25 and 2026-08-26, by hand from two sessions, and a grep of tests/ at every commit in this repository's history finds nothing, because a session that types into a screen leaves nothing in tests/.

THE CARD SAID TO ENUMERATE THE PREFIXES FROM THE TEST SOURCES AND NOT GUESS. Done, and the honest result is that the test sources yield exactly one family, TEST-, as TEST-IN-, TEST-OUT-, TEST-DASH- and TEST-EXT-. The two CRITIC-RACE prefixes are not in any test source and could not have been. Their authority is docs/reports/critic-wave1.md and docs/reports/forensics-20260826-product-count.md, which records CRITIC-RACE-1787702980667 at 2026-08-26 00:09:40+00. That is stated on each registry row rather than left for someone to rediscover.

SO THE PREFIXES ARE NOW ROWS, NOT PREDICATES. rc_reset_sku_prefixes carries one row per marker with the provenance that justifies it, and every predicate reads that one table. The next prefix found by forensics is a row and a line of provenance instead of an edit somebody has to make in nine places consistently.

SELF-ASSERTING, AND WHY THE OLD GRIDS WERE NOT ENOUGH. The file printed numbers and a human decided. That decision was made at the end of a long transaction against live client data by someone told in advance what the numbers should be. Worse, one of the numbers could not disagree with itself: PRE MIXED and POST MIXED were both read from the same frozen temporary table, so they matched whatever the run did. The new assertion 20 counts MIXED survivors in the live tables, and a mutated copy that deletes a mixed order now fails it. That is the difference between a check and a decoration.

THE GATE IS A PLAIN SELECT AND MUST STAY ONE. It casts a message to integer on the failing path, which raises, aborts the transaction and exits psql non-zero. The obvious alternative, DO $$ ... RAISE EXCEPTION $$, was rejected: DoStmt carries its body as an opaque string literal, so parse-reset-sql.mjs, the only thing standing between this file and the client's data, could no longer see an INSERT or a DROP written inside it. A prettier error message is not worth a hole in the inspection. The cast target is a subquery rather than a literal because PostgreSQL constant-folds a literal cast at planning time and would raise on the passing path; verified on 16.15.

NOTHING IN THE PARSER WAS WEAKENED. The card allowed CHECK 4 to be extended if an assertion needed a forbidden kind, and required a halt rather than a weakening. Neither was necessary: the assertions are CreateTableAsStmt and SelectStmt, kinds the file already allowed, so ALLOWED_KINDS and FORBIDDEN_KINDS are byte-identical. CHECK 9 was ADDED, and it is what stops the self-asserting property being removed later: without it, deleting the gate leaves a file that runs all eleven deletes and commits whatever it found while checks 1 to 8 still pass.

PROVEN AGAINST A REAL POSTGRESQL, WHICH THIS FILE HAD NEVER BEEN. P2-15 shipped its SQL with the card admitting "there is no PostgreSQL binary and no running Docker on this machine, so no parser has seen this SQL". Docker is on this machine now. All twelve migrations apply unmodified onto a plain postgres:16 over a small shim for the objects Supabase provides, and the reset was run against a fixture, then against four mutated copies of itself, then twice in a row. THE SHIM IS THE REQUIREMENT WORTH RECORDING: roles anon, authenticated and service_role, schemas auth and storage, auth.users, auth.uid, auth.role, storage.buckets and storage.objects. With those, this repository's schema is reproducible locally by anyone, which is the capability escalation E3 was asking for.

WHY THIS CARD IS BLOCKED AND NOT SHIPPED. Step 4 of the dispatch was to run it against the phase 2 database. That is eleven DELETE statements against the client's project, and CLAUDE.md 8.6 forbids a terminal auto-applying a statement set containing DELETE with no exceptions and no judgement call. cards.notes:
AUTHORED 2026-08-28 FROM AN OWNER DISPATCH. This card writes nothing new. It commits things that were already true and already decided, and were sitting in a chat window.

THE FAILURE THIS REPAIRS IS THE ONE decisions/inbox.md ALREADY NAMES. Its own preamble says 'An answer that is not in this file is not a ruling. A verbal yes that was never pasted here does not exist, because the next session cannot see it.' That rule was written about answers. The same thing happened to a RUN. Ivan executed the reset against the client's database on 2026-08-28, it was ratified in the strategy chat, and none of it was committed. The cost was immediate and it was paid twice in one day: two later dispatches were written against a record that did not exist. One asserted that P2-15 had run and that the grids were in its evidence, while the card carried evidence null and was blocked; the terminal that received it verified before building, found the premise absent, did the buildable work and refused the destructive step. That refusal was correct and this card does not overturn it. It removes the condition that made it necessary.

THE INSTITUTIONAL FIX IS R-047, AND IT IS NOT 'TRUST THE TERMINAL MORE'. The reason a terminal could not be allowed to run a destructive script was never that terminals are careless. It was that the safety of the old file depended on a human reading a grid at the end of a long transaction, having been told in advance what the numbers should be. That is a bad control whoever performs it, and this very run is the demonstration: one number was not what the operator had been told to expect, and the run committed anyway. It committed correctly, for reasons R-048 records, but correctness by judgement is not a control. R-047 therefore attaches the permission to A PROPERTY OF THE FILE rather than to a person, a card or a session: explicit transaction, assertions evaluated in SQL, commit only on all-pass, and the terminal never chooses. A script that cannot commit a wrong outcome is safer in a terminal's hands than a script that can is in anyone's.

WHAT WAS DELIBERATELY NOT WEAKENED. CLAUDE.md 8.6's 'no exceptions, no judgement call, no it is obviously safe here' survives verbatim and still governs every migration and every script without embedded assertions, which is every script in this repository except one. Migrations are explicitly out of scope of the exception. The grant dies three ways: P2-13 revokes it with section 8, first real client data ends it regardless, and it reaches the phase 2 database only.

THE CONFLICT WITH R-044 IS REAL AND IS STATED RATHER THAN SMOOTHED. R-044, ruled the same day, records that P2-13 permanently removes any terminal's ability to open a database connection, and adds P2-19 to P2-13's depends_on on exactly that reasoning. R-047 opens a connection R-044 describes as closed. R-047 supersedes it FOR ASSERTION-BEARING SCRIPTS ONLY and only in the window before P2-13. R-044's capability edge, its ordering argument and its account of the end state are all untouched and all still correct.

STEP 5 WAS NOT PERFORMED, AND THAT IS NOT A HALT. The dispatch said PR #83 was open and that c97e48e had landed its tree as an ordinary fast-forward rather than a PR merge, which is why the record was stale. Both named verifications passed: R-039 to R-046 are each present exactly once on main, and the TRIAGE report is on main. The action did not survive contact: #83 is MERGED, at 2026-08-28T16:43:06Z, and the GitHub API names c97e48e as #83's own mergeCommit. A squash merge produces a single-parent commit, which is why it looks like a fast-forward in the log and is not one. A merged pull request cannot be closed unmerged, and there was no stale record to repair. The halt clause was scoped to the verifications failing; they passed, so the card completed and the action was reported as inapplicable. Nothing was done to #83.

THIS IS THE THIRD DISPATCH IN A ROW CARRYING A PREMISE THE REPOSITORY DID NOT SUPPORT, and the pattern is worth naming rather than absorbing: each time, the premise was about SOMETHING HAVING BEEN RECORDED, and each time the thing had happened but the record had not. Verifying before building caught all three at no cost. The general rule is already in this repository twice, in the inbox preamble and in CLAUDE.md 9b, and it is the same rule: if it is not committed, the next session cannot see it, and the next session is where the cost lands.

EVERY CHANGED PATH OR THE GRANT IS OFF, AND THERE IS NO PARTIAL VERSION. One file outside the role's set removes the grant for the whole pull request, whatever that file is and however small the change to it. Do not reason about whether the stray file mattered; that reasoning is the thing being removed.

WHEN THE ROLE IS AMBIGUOUS, THE NARROWER SET APPLIES. A session that booted as EXECUTOR but is editing the harness is not POC-BUILDER for the purposes of this table. The role is the one the session declared in its first message under CLAUDE.md section 1, and nothing else.

A REPORT COMMIT RIDES WITH THE WORK IT DOCUMENTS AND DOES NOT WIDEN THE SET. CLAUDE.md 9b puts a report in `docs/reports/`, which is inside EXECUTOR's set. A pull request carrying application code plus its report is an application-code pull request and keeps the full section 5b gate; the report does not make it mergeable.

GREEN MEANS GREEN ON THE HEAD SHA, RESOLVED THE STRICT WAY EVERY TIME. A conflicting pull request triggers zero workflows and `gh pr checks` will then report all-pass on leftover contexts from an earlier sha. Verify that a `quality` run exists for the exact head sha and concluded success. A pending check is not green, an absent check is not green, and an inherited check is not green.

A PULL REQUEST THAT MIXES TWO ROLES' SETS IS NOT SELF-MERGEABLE BY EITHER. The grant is per role, and neither role holds the union.

NOTHING HERE OVERRIDES SECTION 3'S OTHER RULES. No pushes to main, no force pushes, no self-invented scope. This clause adds a merge authority and subtracts no discipline.
cards.notes:
AUTHORED AND SHIPPED 2026-08-28 BY AUTHOR, FROM AN OWNER DISPATCH, under ruling R-049. The card, the ruling and the CLAUDE.md amendment are one pull request because all three are the same decision and a board edit landed apart from the rule it describes is a board that lies.

WHAT THIS ACTUALLY CHANGES IS NARROWER THAN IT READS, AND THE NARROWNESS IS THE POINT. Application code already self-merges: section 5b has said since R-002 that cards ship on green_self_merge, which is the green quality check AND the card's named acceptance spec passing. The gap this closes is the pull request that has NO CARD and therefore no acceptance line: a report, a ruling commit, a board edit, a dispatch output. Three of those landed on 2026-08-28 and not one of them had a rule saying who could merge it. So the clause drops the acceptance half of 5b, and drops it only for changes whose content the quality job can already inspect in full.

THE GRANT WAS CHECKED FOR VACUOUSNESS BEFORE IT WAS WRITTEN, WHICH IS THE STEP THAT NEARLY MADE IT WORTHLESS. A self-merge grant conditioned on a green check is only worth the check. On a repository whose workflow carries a `paths:` filter, a documentation-only pull request is SKIPPED and reports success in seconds, so "merge when quality is green" would mean "merge whenever the checks did not run". That is not the case here and it was verified rather than assumed: quality.yml triggers on `pull_request` with no filter of any kind. The acceptance line keeps that grep permanently, and section 3.1 states that adding a path filter kills the clause in the same pull request that adds it.

THE DISPATCH'S PATH LIST HAD TWO REDUNDANCIES AND THEY ARE RESOLVED RATHER THAN COPIED FORWARD. `run.sh` is `scripts/poc/run.sh`, already inside `scripts/poc/`. `docs/board/` is already inside `docs/`. `DESIGN.md` is `docs/poc/DESIGN.md`, and `git ls-files` finds no other file of that name. It does not name AUTHOR, and TRIAGE's authority is unchanged: DOCTRINE-TRIAGE lets it merge its own rulings pull request and no other. So an AUTHOR pull request, INCLUDING THE ONE THAT SHIPS THIS CARD, still goes to Ivan. Widening a grant to a role the owner did not name is escalation item 5, so the gap is recorded here and left open rather than closed by inference. If the intent was that documentation-shaped work stops queueing behind the owner, AUTHOR is the role that writes most of it and the grant does not currently reach it.

cards.defaults:
A PREMISE THAT CANNOT BE VERIFIED IN THE REPOSITORY IS TREATED AS ABSENT, NOT AS PROBABLY FINE. This is the operative form of the rule for every terminal, not only TRIAGE. Check the premise, then build. When a dispatch says something has happened, find it committed before acting on it, and when it is not there, say so and do the part that does not depend on it.

AN UNVERIFIABLE PREMISE DOES NOT HALT THE WHOLE CARD. Do everything that does not depend on it, report the absence precisely, and refuse only the step that actually rested on it. Halting the rest is how a record repair waits another day.

WHEN THE ESCALATION LIST AND ANY UNCOMMITTED DOCUMENT DISAGREE, THE LIST IN DOCTRINE-TRIAGE GOVERNS TERMINALS. Do not open an untracked file to decide what may be decided. If the disagreement matters, it is a card.

RATIFYING A DEVIATION IS NOT ESCALATION ITEM 9. Item 9 is acceptance sign-off, meaning declaring a card, a wave or a phase accepted for the client. Ruling that a terminal's deviation from its card was correct is section 1 work and TRIAGE does it.

A RULING IS NEVER EDITED TO FIX A WRONG PREMISE. A corrected premise is a NEW dated ruling that supersedes by id. This card's own three corrections are inside R-050 as corrections, not as edits to anything earlier.

WHEN IN DOUBT ABOUT WHETHER SOMETHING IS ON THE TEN-ITEM LIST, IT IS NOT. The list is closed and exhaustive by design, and a cautious reading that escalates a borderline case reintroduces exactly the discretion the closure removed.
cards.notes:
AUTHORED AND SHIPPED 2026-08-28 BY AUTHOR, FROM AN OWNER DISPATCH, under ruling R-050.

THE DISPATCH CARRIED THREE PREMISES AND ALL THREE WERE WRONG. Each was checked against the committed record before anything was written, and the substance of the grant survives all three. They are recorded because a card describing the chat-is-not-authority failure while itself repeating uncommitted claims would be the failure.

FIRST, THE ESCALATION LIST IS NOT NARROWED, BECAUSE IT WAS ALREADY THIS LIST AND ALREADY CLOSED. DOCTRINE-TRIAGE section 6 has carried a CLOSED list of nine since AUT-2, opening with "The list is CLOSED. Everything on it goes to Ivan." Nine of the dispatch's ten items were already on it, item for item. The dispatch therefore WIDENS the list by exactly one and narrows nothing. The new item is launch timing, which is genuinely absent from the nine and is genuinely the owner's. Recording this as a narrowing would have left a future reader believing TRIAGE's authority grew on this date; it did not.

SECOND, THE CITED AUTHORITY DOES NOT RESOLVE. "RC-PROJECT-RULES section 2" cannot be followed by a terminal: the file is not tracked in this repository at any commit, it sits in the owner's Downloads folder, and its headings are unnumbered, so section 2 by position is its COMMUNICATION FORMAT heading rather than any list of owner decisions. The matching content is under its OWNER VS DELEGATED heading, the seventh. That document's own first rule is that ground truth is committed repository files only, so citing it as the boundary of a terminal's authority would break the rule it states. The list is written out in DOCTRINE-TRIAGE instead of pointed at.

THIRD, IT WAS THREE DISPATCHES WITH ABSENT PREMISES AND ONE REFUSED STEP, NOT TWO REFUSED DISPATCHES. The committed count is in the REC-01 report, section 6: landing PR #83, RST-01 and REC-01 each carried at least one premise the repository did not support. Exactly one action was refused, RST-01's step 4, correctly. One further step, REC-01's step 5, was inapplicable rather than refused. The LEARNINGS entry carries the accurate count.

ITEM 8 KEEPS ITS WORDING AND GAINS A POINTER, BECAUSE R-047 CHANGED A DIFFERENT VERB. R-047 lets a terminal PERFORM a DELETE-class run when the script proves its own outcome. It gave no role authority to DECIDE such a run should happen, which is what item 8 withholds from TRIAGE. Without the pointer, the next reader finds two rules that look opposed and has to guess which one won.

WHY THE NO-HUMAN-INPUT CLAUSE IS WORTH WRITING WHEN IT WAS ALREADY THE DESIGN. It was implied by the list of what TRIAGE may do and by the closed escalation list, and an implication is what a cautious session talks itself out of at two in the morning. It is now a heading.
